\section{Related Work}\label{sec:relwork}

\paragraph{Bytecode-only detectors.}
A large-scale study~\cite{scannerstudy} evaluates 17 vulnerability-analysis
tools across several datasets. Four bytecode tools are evaluated on
4{,}062{,}844 bytecodes from mainnet and testnets; detection quality is
evaluated separately on labelled corpora. COBRA~\cite{cobra} introduces interaction-aware
bytecode embeddings and explicitly targets the unverified-contract
regime; ByteEye~\cite{byteeye} uses a graph neural network for
bytecode-level detection. SmartBugBert
\cite{smartbugbert} combines BERT and TF-IDF on opcode streams,
reaching $F_1\!\approx\!0.91$ in its own evaluation.

\paragraph{Multimodal and multi-agent LLMs.}
Agent4Vul~\cite{agent4vul} fuses a semantic and a bytecode-CFG
branch; LLM-BSCVM~\cite{llmbscvm} uses multi-agent auditing, and
SmartLLaMA~\cite{smartllama} adapts language models for vulnerability
detection. LLM-SmartAudit~\cite{llmmas} proposes and evaluates a multi-agent
auditing framework. The ACM review~\cite{learnSurvey} surveys 61 selected
publications on learning-based detection.

\paragraph{What this literature does not settle.}
These studies differ in representations, labels and evaluation corpora;
their headline scores are not a common benchmark. Here we compare models
on a shared split, report uncertainty for the binary comparison, and
measure exact feature overlap in the earlier split
(Sec.~\ref{sec:leak-v2}).

\section{Dataset and Protocol}\label{sec:data-v2}

\paragraph{Corpus and what a label means.}
We build on the Slither-audited smart-contract corpus of
Rossini~\cite{slitherAudited}, which pairs Etherscan-verified sources with
their deployed EVM bytecode and per-detector Slither reports. A contract is
positive for a class when the corpus records at least one Slither finding
whose detector maps to that class; the mapping from the 39~detector names to
the eight classes ships with our code
(\texttt{data/label\_mappings.json}), and detectors mapped to
\texttt{ignore} are dropped rather than silently folded into \emph{other}.

The mapping is by detector name alone. The released derivative carries only
the eight binary labels, so no severity or confidence filter is applied at
this stage and none can be recovered from it downstream. A positive therefore
means that Slither emitted a finding, not that the finding is reachable or
exploitable, and every metric in this paper should be read as agreement with
that emission. The eight classes are the corpus's own label set, only
partly aligned with the DASP taxonomy: access-control, arithmetic,
bad-randomness, reentrancy and unchecked-calls correspond to DASP categories,
\emph{locked-ether} is a Slither detector name, \emph{double-spending} is not
a DASP category, and DASP's denial-of-service, front-running and
time-manipulation categories have no label here. We keep the corpus's names
rather than renaming them to a taxonomy they do not match.

\paragraph{Deduplication is the load-bearing preprocessing step.}
Different stored instruction sequences can map to the same numeric feature
vector. Removing only exact text duplicates therefore does not prevent
identical model inputs from appearing on both sides of a split. Our earlier
split contains such overlaps, measured below. This is an opportunity for
memorisation rather than a test on a distinct feature vector.
We remove duplicates twice. The first pass drops \vDupsBc{} contracts whose
stored instruction text is identical. Its implementation also attempts to strip a CBOR trailer, but the stored
field is mnemonic text rather than hexadecimal bytecode
(Sec.~\ref{sec:methods}), so that step is inert and the pass is
exact-duplicate removal on instruction text. The second pass drops \vDupsFeat{} contracts
sharing a \vNFeat-dimensional feature vector, leaving \vCorpus{} contracts at
a positive rate of \vPosRate. The second pass enforces distinct inputs for
the numeric-feature models across partitions. It does not establish
independence of contract families.

\subsection{What the earlier split actually leaked}\label{sec:leak-v2}

The published earlier split permits direct measurement of feature overlap
and its distribution across classes.

Of the validation contracts in that split, \vLeakVal{} (\vLeakRate) are
bit-identical in feature space to a training contract --- rows the model
could recognise rather than classify. Broken down by class, the exposure is
strikingly uneven. For \vLeakWorst{}, \vLeakWorstN{} of \vLeakWorstOf{}
validation positives (\vLeakWorstRate) have an exact twin in training; no
other class exceeds \vLeakNextRate. One group contains
\vCloneFam{} feature-identical deployments, which alone account for
\vCloneShare{} of that class in the training split. The text-level pass
did not eliminate that group's repeated numeric representation.

The earlier paper also reports scores for two classes. On \vLeakWorst, the class
with \vLeakWorstRate{} exposure, the earlier version reported per-class
$F_1 = 0.6835$ where the corrected protocol yields \vRareAXgb.
On \emph{bad-randomness}, exposed at
\vRareBLeak{} --- the low end of that range --- it reported $0.6302$ where we now
measure \vRareBXgb. These changes accompanied a change in partition and
evaluation protocol; the earlier validation and current test results are
not a causal estimate of the effect of deduplication. No controlled
deduplication ablation was performed.

Sharing a contaminated split does not guarantee that model comparisons are
unaffected: learners may exploit repeated inputs differently, and macro-$F_1$
gives equal weight to rare and common classes. The overlap audit identifies
the exposure, not the amount by which each model's score was inflated.

\paragraph{Split.}
A stratified \vTrain/\vVal/\vTest{} train/validation/test split (seed
\vSeed) preserves the positive rate to three decimals in every fold. We
assert, as a build-time invariant, that no feature vector occurs in more
than one split; the assertion ships with the code. The binary Optuna search uses training folds;
decision thresholds use validation. \textbf{The test split is read once, after
selection, for the numbers reported below.}

The reference evaluation uses one draw of the split. The bootstrap intervals quantify sampling
variability \emph{within} the \vTest{} test contracts, not variability across
alternative partitions of the corpus. We did not repeat the protocol under
other seeds, so the point estimates carry an unquantified split-to-split
component. The observed \vDlGap~p.p.\ gap and per-class sweep describe this
split; their stability across alternative splits has not been measured.

\section{Methods}\label{sec:methods}

\paragraph{Binary classification.}
Four models on the \vNFeat{} features: LogisticRegression
(\texttt{class\_weight=balanced}), RandomForest (500~trees in the released replay recipe), XGBoost tuned
with Optuna~\cite{optuna} (50~trials, 5-fold stratified CV \emph{inside the
training split}), and CatBoost~\cite{catboost} as an independent boosting
family that also exposes a different feature-importance measure
(PredictionValuesChange). The reference run's fitted models and fit-time
environment were not saved; recipe settings do not recover that missing
provenance.

\paragraph{Multi-label classification.}
The reference pipeline fits LogReg and XGBoost through
\texttt{sklearn.MultiOutputClassifier}, and a native multi-output
RandomForest with 400~trees, to the eight classes of
Sec.~\ref{sec:data-v2}. The latter shares tree partitions across outputs
rather than fitting eight separate forests. We report the saved per-class
scores descriptively. The eight labels refer to the same contracts;
they are not eight independent experimental replications.

\paragraph{Deep-learning comparator.}
A Conv-Transformer --- a depth-2 transformer over a 3-layer 1D-CNN
tokeniser, on 20{,}000-token sequences --- is trained on the same
multi-label split. The ablation covers loss (\texttt{BCE},
$+\!\texttt{pos\_weight}$, focal $\gamma\!=\!2$,
focal$\,+\,$\texttt{pos\_weight}, asymmetric~\cite{asl2021}, threshold
tuning) and architecture (\vDlArch).

\paragraph{Representation caveat.}
A provenance audit of the sequence pipeline found that the historical
converter passed
the hexadecimal \emph{string} to the disassembler without decoding it to
bytes. ASCII values were interpreted as opcodes; the values for
\texttt{a}--\texttt{f} are \texttt{PUSH} instructions that consume subsequent
characters as operands. The fitted token vocabulary contains \vHexVocab{}
entries, with \vHexNamed{} named mnemonics corresponding to hexadecimal
ASCII values. The released cleaning expression removes intermediate
operands, making this path lossy: for example, \texttt{a00a00} and
\texttt{a11a00} both become \texttt{PUSH2 PUSH2 0x3030} before tokenisation.
Unknown-token mapping and length truncation add further possible loss. This
counterexample establishes non-injectivity, not its frequency or effect on
scores in the corpus. The audited numeric-feature extractor instead calls
\texttt{bytes.fromhex} before disassembly and does not have this input-type
error. Every test-split deep-learning number in this paper describes the
legacy sequence pipeline. The released rows carry only that text, and it is
not invertible, since the PUSH operands were removed; the upstream
corpus~\cite{slitherAudited} still carries the deployed bytecode, and the
converter's projection is deterministic, so recomputing it on each of the
\vDecUpstream{} upstream contracts re-attaches the bytecode to every training and validation row by exact
match.
Sec.~\ref{sec:ml-v2} reports the best deep configuration retrained on
those bytes, decoded to one mnemonic per instruction with the PUSH
operands and the metadata trailer removed.

\paragraph{Bootstrap confidence intervals.}
Headline binary metrics carry stratified percentile bootstrap 95\% intervals
over the test split. Where two models are compared, the bootstrap is
\emph{paired} on the difference (Sec.~\ref{sec:binary-v2}): the models see the same contracts, so their errors are correlated.

\paragraph{Security-specific metrics.}
We report MCC~\cite{mcc} alongside $F_1$ because the corpus is \vPosRate{} positive: at that skew $F_1$ can be inflated by predicting the majority class generously, whereas MCC accounts for all four cells of the confusion matrix. We report the false-negative rate explicitly because in security a missed vulnerability is operationally costlier than a false alarm. Beyond
ranking we report PR-AUC, more informative than ROC-AUC for imbalanced
positives~\cite{prauc}, and we note in Sec.~\ref{sec:binary-v2} that top-$k$ recall is bounded by
$K/\pi_{+}$ at this corpus's positive rate and is not reported.

\paragraph{Interpretability.}
We compare XGBoost split gain~\cite{xgboost} with SHAP
TreeExplainer~\cite{shap} attributions from the same protocol-matched refit,
using validation samples for SHAP, not test. Sec.~\ref{sec:ml-v2} reports
the ranking overlap; it does not establish a causal relation to vulnerabilities.

XGBoost with Optuna-tuned hyperparameters reaches $F_1 =$ \vBXGBFone{}
[\vBXGBLo, \vBXGBHi] at a false-negative rate of \vBXGBFnr{}
(Table~\ref{tab:binary-v2}). Tuning used 50 trials optimising mean $F_1$
over a 5-fold stratified cross-validation \emph{inside the training split};
neither validation nor test participated in the search. 

\paragraph{Model comparison requires a paired test.}
Marginal confidence intervals for XGBoost and RandomForest overlap, and it
is tempting — but wrong — to conclude from that overlap that the models are
indistinguishable: the two are evaluated on the \emph{same} contracts, so
their errors are correlated and the marginal intervals are the wrong object.
The reference artifact records a bootstrap mean of the paired difference,
$\overline{\Delta F_1}=\vDeltaFone$, with a percentile 95\% interval
[\vDeltaLo, \vDeltaHi], $P(\Delta>0)$ \vDeltaPgt{}, over \vDeltaB{} resamples, but its fit-time environment
and fitted XGBoost model were not saved. The controlled rerun gives
\vSensDeltaFone{} [\mbox{\vSensDeltaLo}, \mbox{\vSensDeltaHi}],
$P(\Delta>0)=\vSensPgt$ (\vSensB{} resamples), so its interval crosses zero.
Here $P(\Delta>0)$ denotes the fraction of bootstrap replicates with a
positive difference, not a posterior probability or a frequentist $p$-value.
At table level \vSensTableMatches{} models match; only \vSensExactMatches{}
(\vSensExactModel) matches exactly, with all \vTest{} RF scores bit-identical.
For XGBoost the threshold moves \vSensXgbThrRef{}$\to$\vSensXgbThrRerun{}
and $F_1$ \vBXGBFone{}$\to$\vSensXgbFoneRerun. We retain the reference points,
treat the rerun as sensitivity analysis, and do not claim a statistically
resolved advantage across environments. The remaining mechanism is unknown;
versions, threads, platform and the reference run's model state are hypotheses only.

\paragraph{Tier-1 operating envelope on this corpus, and where it does not
apply.}
A false-negative rate of \vBXGBFnr{} is a property of the
validation-selected threshold, and that threshold is permissive: at
precision \vBXGBPrec{} and recall \vBXGBRec{} on a corpus that is \vPosRate{}
positive, the filter forwards $\pi_{+}r/p \approx \vFlagRate$ of all
contracts. The workload reduction is therefore about
\vWorkloadRed$\times$. These are two expressions of the same operating
point. At a positive rate of \vPosRate{} even a perfect ranker recovers at most
$K/\pi_{+}$ of the positives within its top $K\%$, so a smaller forwarding
budget on this corpus cannot buy high recall.

Whether a filter saves useful downstream work depends on deployment
prevalence, transfer of precision and recall, and the cost of missed
findings. We have not measured those quantities on a deployment stream.
The operational argument is therefore conditional, not a demonstrated
benefit outside this corpus.

\section{Multi-Label Results and the Deep Comparator}\label{sec:ml-v2}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{perlabel_f1_heatmap_v2.pdf}
\caption{Per-class $F_1$ on the held-out test split under the v2 protocol:
classical multi-label baselines (left of the first rule) against the
\vDlNConfigs{} Conv-Transformer configurations. Classes are ordered as in Sec.~\ref{sec:data-v2};
\textit{double-spending} is the rarest class and the one on which every model
degrades.}
\label{fig:heatmap-v2}
\end{figure*}

On the eight-class multi-label task, classical XGBoost reaches macro-$F_1 =$
\vMlXgb, RandomForest \vMlRf, and balanced logistic regression \vMlLr{} ---
with the lowest logistic-regression scores on the rare classes. These
scores alone do not identify whether the limitation is the representation,
decision thresholds, optimisation or model capacity.

\paragraph{Deep comparator.}
We train \vDlNConfigs{} Conv-Transformer configurations spanning loss
functions (BCE, positive-weighting, focal, asymmetric, threshold tuning) and
architectures (\vDlArch). Each is trained on
the same training split, early-stopped on an internal carve-out of that
split, and evaluated once on the same held-out test split as the classical
models. The best configuration, \vDlBestName, reaches macro-$F_1 =$
\vDlBest{} (worst \vDlWorst, mean \vDlMean), trailing XGBoost by
\vDlGap~p.p. Every one of these numbers is a result for the legacy token
representation described in Sec.~\ref{sec:methods}, in which the comparator
was fed the hexadecimal text of the bytecode rather than its decoded opcodes.
\vDlCaveat

\paragraph{Decoded opcodes.}
To test whether the representation defect explains that gap, the best
configuration, \vDlBestName, was retrained on the re-attached bytecode of
Sec.~\ref{sec:methods}, decoded to one mnemonic per instruction
(vocabulary \vDecVocab, median \vDecLenMed{} tokens per contract), with
the legacy tokens as the control: same code, seed, rows (\vDecTrainRows{}
training and \vDecValRows{} validation contracts) and internal carve-out,
differing only in the input. Because the test split had already been read,
both runs are scored on the validation split, and the classical model was
refitted and scored there under the same conditions. The decoded input
reaches macro-$F_1 =$ \vDecodedVal, \vDecGapAbs~p.p.\ above the legacy
control (\vLegacyVal) and trailing XGBoost on the same split (\vDecXgbVal)
by \vDecXgbGapAbs~p.p. For this configuration the defect does not explain the gap: with a
correct input the deep model still scores below gradient boosting.
This is a validation-level result for one configuration, not a new
test-split number. The two inputs also differ in length: at the
\vSeqCap-token cap the model reads, the decoded stream fits whole while the
legacy text is cut for \vLegTruncPct{} of training contracts (median
\vLegLenMed{} tokens against \vDecLenMed), so the difference between the arms
is not purely one of meaning. The decoded arm was executed \vDecRunsN{} times in all,
on three machines, with the same code, data and seed; the scores span
\vDecSpread~p.p.\ (lowest \vDecLowest), so the \vDecGapAbs~p.p.\ the decoding
buys is close to that spread and the \vDecXgbGapAbs~p.p.\ still separating it
from gradient boosting is well outside it.

\paragraph{Per-class comparison.}
XGBoost scores higher in \vDlWins{} classes against \vDlBestName{} and
against every other deep configuration (Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap-v2});
\vDlLosing{} of \vDlOf{} configurations have lower macro-$F_1$. The classes
share contracts and the configurations share data, so these comparisons are
descriptive and no significance test is applied.

\paragraph{Lowest observed scores occur on rare classes.}
Both the rarest classes are the hardest for every model in the comparison.
\vRareAName{} accounts for \vRareAPrev{} of test contracts and \vRareBName{}
for \vRareBPrev; classical XGBoost reaches \vRareAXgb{} and \vRareBXgb{} on
them, against \vBestLabXgb{} on the most common class,
\vBestLabName. The deep configurations also score lower on these classes
(Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap-v2}). Scarcity is a possible contributor, but this
design does not separate it from label quality, representation loss,
optimisation or capacity. The earlier overlap audit and changed scores
(Sec.~\ref{sec:leak-v2}) do not isolate those effects either.

\paragraph{Interpretability.}
Attributions come from a protocol-matched refit using the recorded XGBoost
hyperparameters on \vShapN{} validation samples; the reference fit
behind Table~\ref{tab:binary-v2}, whose model was not saved, is not being
explained. We use split gain,
which measures the average gain of splits using a feature, and mean absolute
SHAP, which counts how much each feature moves the output.

They share a core and diverge beyond it. \vShapAgree{} of
the top five appear in both lists --- \texttt{external\_call\_count}, \texttt{call\_gas\_limit\_ops} and \texttt{jumpi\_count} --- but the
agreement does not survive lengthening them: the Jaccard overlap
falls from \vJacFive{} at $K=5$ to \vJacFifteen{} at $K=15$.
Two rankings of one fit agreeing on part of their heads is weaker
evidence than a single ordering would suggest, and we report it as
such.

Direction is the more useful signal. Every feature in the SHAP top five except \texttt{conditional\_branching\_ratio} pushes the classifier toward ``vulnerable'' as its value rises,
which is the sign an auditor would predict for external calls and
branching complexity. We note one departure from the earlier
version, which built its account on \texttt{has\_external\_calls}: that
feature leads neither ranking here, while \vShapLead{}
leads the SHAP one. The earlier ranking came from the leaking split,
so the overlap that does exist is worth stating and not worth
leaning on.



\section{Discussion and Future Work}\label{sec:disc}

\paragraph{Why the comparator lost.}
The \vNFeat{} features form a mid-dimensional tabular representation, the
regime in which tree ensembles are reported to outperform deep
networks~\cite{grinsztajn2022,shwartz2022}. The decoded-opcode run of
Sec.~\ref{sec:ml-v2} removes the other candidate explanation at validation
level: with a correct input the best deep configuration moves
\vDecGapAbs~p.p.\ relative to its legacy control and still trails XGBoost
by \vDecXgbGapAbs~p.p. What is measured on the test split remains a result
for the legacy representation; what the validation run adds is that
correcting the representation does not reverse the ordering.

\paragraph{Future work.}
Potential comparators include bytecode graph models such as
ByteEye~\cite{byteeye}, COBRA's recurrent sequence and interface-feature
model~\cite{cobra}, and multimodal or multi-agent approaches. COBRA and
ByteEye do not require verified source at inference; their resource needs
have not been measured against this pipeline. Before extending the model
comparison on the test split, the corpus needs re-splitting by contract
family and a partition that excludes every contract of the present test
split; the decoded input of Sec.~\ref{sec:ml-v2} then needs a test-level
run under that partition.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
\textbf{(i)~Target and deployment validity.} Agreement with mapped Slither
findings is not recall against independently confirmed vulnerabilities.
Without independent labels, neither an improvement over Slither nor a
numerical ceiling imposed by its errors has been established. Evaluation
against curated or mutation-based labels, such as SolidiFI~\cite{solidifi},
would need matched label semantics. Transfer to unverified deployments and
downstream triage benefit also remain unmeasured.
\textbf{(ii)~One split and incomplete fit provenance.} The bootstrap covers
sampling within one test split, not alternative partitions. Reference
artifacts preserve scores but not fitted models or fit-time environment; the
rerun matches \vSensTableMatches{} models at table level and
\vSensExactMatches{} exactly, moving the paired interval across zero.
Compiler version is not stratified and contract families are not grouped,
so dependence beyond exact feature twins, including template families
whose members differ in a few features, is unmeasured.
\textbf{(iii)~Dependent comparisons.} Class scores and configuration scores
share observations. We retain their ordering descriptively rather than
treating them as independent replications. The binary paired interval
answers a within-split question and does not resolve that broader uncertainty.
\textbf{(iv)~Attribution agreement is modest.} Split gain and mean
absolute SHAP, computed on the same protocol-matched refit, share three of their top five
features and less beyond that. We report the overlap rather than treat it
as corroboration.
\textbf{(v)~Legacy sequence representation.} The deep comparator's
test-split inputs were produced by disassembling hexadecimal text without
decoding it (Sec.~\ref{sec:methods}); those results characterise that
representation. The decoded-opcode check covers one configuration under one
seed, scored on the validation split; it is not a test-split result. On \vFeatRows{} sampled
contracts, \vFeatExact{} of the \vNFeat{} released feature columns are exactly
an affine image of the audited extractor's output on the re-attached
bytecode; the rest are constant across that sample rather than
contradicted, and no column was checked on every row.
\textbf{(vi)~Cost.} Wall-clock training time survives for \vDlTimeN{} of the
\vDlTimeOf{} deep configurations (\vDlTimeLo{} to \vDlTimeHi{}~s on a GPU).
In the decoded-opcode run the classical multi-label fit took \vXgbFitS~s on
\vXgbCpus{} CPU cores, and the deep configuration \vDecodedMin~min of
\vDecGpu{} time over \vDecodedEpochs{} epochs on the same machine; inference
cost was not measured, so no throughput comparison is drawn.
